6880:
To "get someone's drift" means to understand the general point or the hidden meaning of what someone is saying, even when they haven't said everything out loud or haven't been completely direct.

Think of it this way: sometimes people don't say exactly what they mean. They hint at it, talk around it, or explain it partially. If you "get their drift," you've understood where they were going with their words — you've caught the underlying message.

Simple one-line definition: "Do you get my drift?" = "Do you understand what I'm trying to say?"
Breaking Down the Word "Drift"

To truly understand this idiom, you need to understand what the word "drift" means here.

In everyday language, "drift" means the slow movement of something in a general direction — like snow drifting in the wind, or a boat drifting on a river current. You don't always know the exact path, but you can see the general direction it's heading.

When applied to language and ideas, "drift" means the general direction or tendency of someone's thoughts or words. It's the underlying current of what they're communicating — not the exact words, but the overall message those words are moving toward.

So when you "get someone's drift," you are catching that current — you're following the direction of their thinking and arriving at the intended meaning.
The Structure of the Idiom

This idiom can be used in a few slightly different forms:

1. "Get my drift" — the most common form, used as a question or statement.

"I'm not saying you're wrong, but... you get my drift?"

(= "Do you understand what I'm implying?")

2. "Get the drift" — used when referring to a general idea or a piece of content (like a speech, a book, a conversation).

"I didn't read every word, but I got the drift of what he was saying."

(= "I understood the general idea.")

3. "Catch my/someone's drift" — "catch" can be used instead of "get" with the exact same meaning.

"She gave him a long look. He caught her drift immediately."

(= "He immediately understood what she meant without her saying it.")

4. "You/I get the drift" — a statement (not a question) confirming understanding.

"He kept glancing at the clock. I got the drift — it was time to leave."
How Is It Different from Just "Understanding"?

This is a key distinction. "Get someone's drift" is not the same as simply understanding something that was said clearly.

If your teacher writes 2 + 2 = 4 on the board and you understand it, you wouldn't say "I got your drift." That's just ordinary understanding.

"Get someone's drift" is specifically used when:

  • The message is implied rather than stated
  • The speaker is hinting at something without being direct
  • The explanation is incomplete, and you're figuring out the rest
  • The meaning is indirect, subtle, or partially hidden

Ordinary understanding: "She told me to be quiet. I understood."
Getting someone's drift: "She didn't say anything, but she gave me that look. I got her drift."
Everyday Examples in Context

Example 1 — At work:

"Look, I'm not saying your report was bad, but... the client called us three times this week. You get my drift?"

Here, the boss isn't directly saying "your report caused problems," but the implication is clear. If you "get the drift," you understand you need to do better.

Example 2 — Between friends:

"He kept talking about how tired he was, how busy his schedule was, how little free time he had. I got the drift — he didn't want to come to the party."

The friend never said "I don't want to come." But by picking up on all the hints, you understood his true message.

Example 3 — A parent to a child:

"I don't have to spell out every rule in this house. Do you get my drift?"

The parent is saying: "You already know what I mean, so don't pretend you don't."

Example 4 — Reading or listening:

"The professor's lecture was fast and complex, but I got the drift of his argument."

Here, you may not have caught every single detail, but you understood the main point or direction of his thinking.
Tone and Register — When Is This Idiom Used?

This idiom is informal and conversational. You would use it in:

  • Casual conversations between friends, family, or colleagues
  • Informal writing (text messages, informal emails, dialogue in stories)
  • Situations where you want to sound natural and relaxed

You would not typically use it in:

  • Formal business reports
  • Academic essays
  • Official or legal documents
A Subtle but Important Nuance — The "Warning" Use

One very common use of this idiom carries a mild warning or threat — spoken or unspoken. When someone says "Do you get my drift?" after implying a consequence, it often means: "I'm not going to spell it out for you, but you'd better understand and act accordingly."

"I'd hate to have to call your parents about this. Do you get my drift?"

This isn't a friendly question about comprehension. It's a veiled warning. The speaker expects you to read between the lines and take the implied threat seriously.
Origin of the Idiom

The word "drift" in the sense of "meaning" or "intention of speech" has been part of the English language since at least the 16th century. Writers like Shakespeare used the word "drift" to refer to the intended direction or purpose of an argument or speech.

Over time, this sense of "drift" — the underlying direction of thought — merged into the everyday expression "get one's drift," which became widely popular in modern informal English.
Similar Idioms with the Same Meaning

These expressions all mean roughly the same thing as "get someone's drift":

  • "Read between the lines" — understand the hidden meaning in what's said or written
  • "Take the hint" — understand an indirect suggestion
  • "Get the picture" — understand the overall situation
  • "Catch on" — begin to understand something
  • "See where someone is going" — follow the direction of someone's thinking
  • "Get the message" — understand the real meaning, often a warning or instruction
How to Remember It Forever

Here's a simple mental image to lock this in your memory:

Imagine someone is floating in a boat on a river. They're not paddling in a straight line — they're drifting, slowly moving in a general direction. If you're watching from the bank, you can see where they're heading even though they're not going in a perfectly straight path.

That boat is the speaker's words. The river current is their true meaning. To "get the drift" is to see where that boat is heading — to understand the general direction and destination of their communication.
Quick Summary

AspectDetail
Core MeaningTo understand the general or implied point of what someone is saying
Key Word"Drift" = the underlying direction/tendency of thought or speech
RegisterInformal, conversational
Most Common Form"Do you get my drift?"
Also Used As"Catch the drift," "get the drift of something"
Special UseOften implies a veiled warning or hint

In short: "Get one's drift" means to understand the implied or general point of what someone is saying, especially when they haven't been completely direct. The word "drift" refers to the underlying direction of someone's thoughts — like a current carrying words toward a meaning. It's an informal expression, most commonly heard as "Do you get my drift?", and it often carries a light warning tone. You can also say "catch the drift" or "get the drift of something" with the same meaning.
6881:
To "get your ducks in a row" means to organize everything properly and be fully prepared before starting something. When someone has their ducks in a row, they have handled all the details, made all the necessary plans, and are ready to move forward without any loose ends.

Think of it simply as: "Get yourself organized and ready."
The Literal Picture Behind the Idiom

To understand an idiom, it always helps to picture what it literally describes.

Imagine a mother duck walking with her baby ducklings (called ducklings) behind her. The babies naturally line up in a neat, orderly, single-file row and follow her in a tidy, organized manner. Everything is in order. Everything is in its right place. There is no chaos.

Now contrast that with ducklings scattered all over the place, going in random directions — that is the image of disorganization and unpreparedness.

So when you "get your ducks in a row," you are taking those scattered, chaotic ducklings and lining them up neatly — meaning you are taking your messy, unorganized tasks, responsibilities, or plans and putting them all in proper order.
How It Is Used in Real Life

This idiom is used when someone needs to sort out their affairs, complete preparations, or handle pending matters before they can move on to the next step. It is extremely common in everyday English, especially in professional, academic, and personal contexts.

It often carries a sense of "don't rush in unprepared." The underlying message is: take the time to organize first, then act.

The idiom changes slightly depending on who is doing the organizing:

  • I need to get my ducks in a row. (yourself)
  • She needs to get her ducks in a row. (a third person)
  • We need to get our ducks in a row. (a group)
  • He finally has his ducks in a row. (already organized — note "has" instead of "get")
  • Get your ducks in a row! (a command/advice to someone)

The key verb here is usually "get" (to achieve the state of being organized) or "have" (already being in that organized state).

Here are several examples across different situations so the meaning becomes crystal clear:

At work:
"Before we present this project to the board, let's get our ducks in a row — we need the data, the slides, and the budget report all ready."

Before a big life event:
"She wanted to get her ducks in a row before applying for a mortgage — she paid off her debts and saved a larger down payment first."

Giving advice:
"You can't just walk into a job interview unprepared. Get your ducks in a row first — research the company, practice your answers, and dress professionally."

Describing someone who is already organized:
"Don't worry about Marcus handling the event — he always has his ducks in a row."

Describing disorganization:
"The launch failed because the team hadn't gotten their ducks in a row. Important approvals were still missing."

It is important to understand a few things this idiom does not imply:

  • It does not mean being perfect. It just means being sufficiently organized and prepared.
  • It does not always mean you must take a very long time to prepare. Sometimes "getting your ducks in a row" takes five minutes; sometimes it takes months. The time involved depends on the situation.
  • It is not a negative expression. It is neutral to positive — it encourages smart, thoughtful preparation.

This phrase has a practical, no-nonsense tone. When someone says it, they are usually being sensible and forward-thinking. It is the language of someone who values preparation over impulsive action.

It can also occasionally carry a mild warning — for example, if a boss says "We need to get our ducks in a row before the client arrives," it signals that things are currently not ready and that must change urgently.
Where the Idiom Likely Came From

The exact origin is not pinned down with absolute certainty, but there are two popular theories:

Theory 1 — Mother duck and ducklings: As described above, the image of ducklings following their mother in an orderly line. This is the most widely accepted and visually intuitive explanation.

Theory 2 — Billiards/Pool: In early pool and billiard games, the targets were sometimes informally called "ducks." Arranging them in a neat row before a game meant everything was set up and ready to play. "Getting your ducks in a row" would then mean setting up all the targets in their correct positions.

Both theories point to the same core idea: neatness, order, and readiness.

The phrase became widely used in American English throughout the 20th century and is now a staple expression in everyday speech.
Similar Idioms With the Same Meaning

English has several other expressions that mean roughly the same thing. Knowing them will help you recognize the idea even when this exact phrase isn't used:

  • "Get your act together" — organize yourself and stop being chaotic
  • "Dot your i's and cross your t's" — attend to every small but important detail
  • "Have everything in order" — be fully prepared and organized
  • "Lay the groundwork" — do the preparatory work before starting
  • "Get your house in order" — sort out your own affairs before acting

QuestionAnswer

Simply put: "get your ducks in a row" = get organized and fully prepared. It is used before starting something important. It tells you — or someone else — to handle all the moving parts, pending tasks, and details first, so that when you take action, you do so smoothly, confidently, and without unnecessary surprises.

It is one of the most practical and widely used idioms in English, and now you know everything about it — its meaning, its grammar, its origin, its tone, its examples, and its cousins.
6882:
"Get one's own back" means to take revenge on someone who has harmed, cheated, or wronged you — to do something back to them that makes you feel that justice has been served. It is about evening the score.

The key idea is this: someone did something bad to you first, and now you do something back to them in return. It restores the balance in your mind. You feel that you have "gotten back" what was taken from you — your dignity, your advantage, your pride, or your sense of fairness.

Think of it as a personal settling of accounts. You were wronged. Now you've responded. Now you're even.

This idiom makes beautiful sense when you look at it word by word.

  • "Get" = to obtain or win back.
  • "One's own" = what belongs to you — your pride, your position, your advantage.
  • "Back" = the return of something you lost.

So literally, you are getting back what is your own — something that was taken from you unfairly. The "something" is often not a physical object. It is your pride, your dignity, your equal standing with another person.
The Tone — Is It Serious or Light?

This is very important. "Get one's own back" sits in the middle ground of revenge. It is not violent, not criminal, and not dramatic. It describes a relatively mild, personal act of retaliation — the kind of thing ordinary people do in everyday life.

It can even be used in a slightly playful or humorous tone, especially in British English. For example, if your little brother always beats you at board games and one day you finally win, you might say with a grin: "Ha! I finally got my own back!" Nobody is in danger. Nobody is hurt. It is just satisfaction.

However, it can also be used in more serious situations — like an employee who was treated unfairly by a manager, and who later finds a way to expose that manager's dishonesty. The tone depends entirely on the context.

This is primarily a British English idiom. You will hear and read it constantly in the United Kingdom, Ireland, Australia, and other parts of the English-speaking world that have been influenced by British English. It appears in casual conversation, novels, newspapers, and television.

In American English, people more commonly say "get back at someone" or "get even" to express the same idea. However, educated American speakers do understand "get one's own back" perfectly well.

Reading idioms in context is the best way to understand them. Here are varied examples that show the full range of how this idiom is used:

Example 1 — Workplace:
"My boss took credit for my idea in front of the whole company. I got my own back when I was promoted over him the following year."
→ The speaker felt wronged. Later, a natural event gave them the upper hand. They felt satisfied.

Example 2 — Friendly competition:
"She beat me at tennis three times in a row, but I got my own back in today's match."
→ Playful. No hard feelings. Just satisfaction at finally winning.

Example 3 — Childhood:
"My older sister used to hide my toys. I got my own back by telling Mum she was the one who broke the vase."
→ A sibling rivalry. Mild revenge. Common in everyday storytelling.

Example 4 — Business:
"After the company stole his design, he got his own back by launching a competing product that took half their customers."
→ More serious, but still within normal professional rivalry.

Example 5 — Future intention:
"Just you wait. I'll get my own back someday."
→ A warning or a promise of future retaliation. Very common structure.

Example 6 — Third person:
"She was determined to get her own back on the people who had spread lies about her."
→ Shows the structure with "her own back" — the possessive changes based on who the subject is.
The Grammar — How to Use It Correctly

The possessive pronoun in the middle of the idiom always changes to match the subject of the sentence. This is something learners often miss.

  • I will get my own back.
  • He got his own back.
  • She got her own back.
  • They got their own back.
  • We will get our own back.

The structure is: Subject + get/got + [possessive] + own back + (on + person)

The "on + person" part (meaning: on whom you are taking revenge) is optional. You can say it or leave it out depending on whether the person is already understood from context.

  • "I got my own back." ✅ (The person is already known from context.)
  • "I got my own back on him." ✅ (Explicitly naming the target.)

The verb "get" is conjugated normally across tenses:

  • Present: "I am trying to get my own back."
  • Past: "She got her own back."
  • Future: "He will get his own back one day."
  • Perfect: "They have finally gotten their own back."
What Makes It Different From Pure "Revenge"?

The word revenge in English often carries a heavy, dark, sometimes obsessive feeling. Think of dramatic stories, long-held grudges, and serious harm being done.

"Get one's own back" is lighter than revenge. It suggests a personal, proportionate response to a personal wrong. It is about restoring balance, not about destruction. You get back what belongs to you — your fair standing — and then you move on. The emotional weight is more like satisfaction than fury.

This distinction matters for choosing the right word. If someone's neighbour borrowed their lawnmower and never returned it, and they respond by quietly refusing to help that neighbour in future, you would say: "I got my own back." You would not dramatically say: "I took revenge." That would sound out of proportion.

These mean roughly the same thing and are useful to know alongside this idiom:

  • Get back at someone — American, very common: "I'll get back at him for what he did."
  • Get even (with someone) — Very common globally: "She waited years to get even with him."
  • Pay someone back — "He paid them back for every insult they threw at him."
  • Turn the tables (on someone) — To reverse a situation so you now have the advantage.
  • Give someone a taste of their own medicine — To do to someone the same bad thing they did to you.
  • Settle a score — To resolve an old grievance.

Among all of these, "get one's own back" is the most distinctly British and the most personal in feeling.
A Simple Way to Remember It Forever

Imagine someone stole your favourite pen. You feel the loss. Later, you find an equally clever way to take your pen back from them. You now have your own thing back.

Now apply that image not to a pen, but to your pride, dignity, or advantage — things that cannot be physically stolen but can absolutely be taken from you by someone's actions.

When you restore that, you have gotten your own back.

That image — of reclaiming something that is rightfully yours — is the heart of this idiom, and it will never leave you once you picture it.
6883:
When something "gets out of hand," it means it has become impossible to control or manage. A situation, a person, or a problem that was once manageable has now grown too big, too wild, or too serious to handle.

Think of it this way — imagine you are holding a ball of yarn. As long as you hold it tightly, it's neat and under control. But the moment it slips from your grip and rolls away, unraveling in all directions, it has gotten out of hand. You can no longer manage it.
Where Did This Idiom Come From?

The origin of this idiom goes back hundreds of years to horse riding and horse training. A rider controls a horse by holding the reins — the long straps connected to the horse's bridle — firmly in their hands. When the horse is calm and obedient, it is said to be "in hand," meaning it is fully under the rider's control.

But if the horse suddenly becomes wild, rears up, or bolts away, it "gets out of hand" — literally escaping the grip of the person trying to control it.

Over time, people began using this expression beyond horses, applying it to any situation, person, or problem that escapes control. Today, you don't need to know anything about horses to use or understand this idiom. It is used in everyday life constantly.
The Core Idea to Always Remember

"In hand" = under control. "Out of hand" = no longer under control.

This is the heart of the idiom. Whenever something crosses the line from manageable to unmanageable, you can say it has gotten out of hand.
How It Is Used — Grammatical Forms

The idiom is flexible and can be used in different tenses depending on what you want to say.

Present tense — to describe something happening right now:
"This situation is getting out of hand."

Past tense — to describe something that already became uncontrollable:
"The argument got out of hand very quickly."

Future / warning form — to warn that something could become uncontrollable:
"We need to act now before things get out of hand."

The most common forms you will hear are "got out of hand" (past) and "getting out of hand" (present continuous, used as a warning or observation).
What Kind of Things Can "Get Out of Hand"?

Almost anything can get out of hand. Here are the main categories:

Situations and Events
A party, a meeting, a protest, a game, a celebration — any event that starts normally but slowly turns chaotic.

Arguments and Conflicts
A small disagreement between two people that turns into a huge fight.

Emotions
Anger, laughter, excitement, or grief that grows so intense it becomes overwhelming.

People or Groups
A child who becomes disobedient, a crowd that turns violent, a group of students that becomes impossible to manage.

Problems
Debt, a fire, a disease, a rumor — any problem that was small at first but has now grown too large to manage easily.
Examples in Real Sentences

These examples will show you exactly how native speakers use this idiom naturally:

  1. "The debate started calmly, but it quickly got out of hand when both sides started shouting."
  2. "The kids were getting out of hand, so their mother turned off the TV and sent them to bed."
  3. "The small kitchen fire got out of hand before the firefighters arrived."
  4. "His spending is getting out of hand — he needs to create a budget immediately."
  5. "What started as a small student protest got completely out of hand by the evening."
  6. "The rumors about her got out of hand, and she had to make a public statement to correct them."
  7. "Let's resolve this issue now before it gets out of hand."

Notice in the last example how the idiom is used as a warning — one of its most common and powerful uses.
The Word "Completely" — A Common Companion

You will very often hear people say "completely out of hand" or "totally out of hand" to add emphasis and show that the situation has become severely uncontrollable, not just mildly so.

"The party got completely out of hand — the neighbours called the police."
The Gradual Nature of This Idiom

One important and subtle thing to understand about this idiom is that it almost always implies a process — something that started under control and then slowly or suddenly lost that control. It's rarely used for things that were never manageable to begin with.

This is why you will often hear phrases like:

  • "before it gets out of hand" (it isn't there yet, but it could be)
  • "it started fine, but then it got out of hand" (it was okay, then it wasn't)
  • "things are getting out of hand" (the process is happening right now)
Words and Phrases That Mean the Same Thing (Synonyms)

If you want to express the same idea in a different way, you can use:

  • spiral out of control — "The crisis spiraled out of control."
  • go haywire — more casual, often used for machines or plans
  • run wild — often used for children or crowds
  • escalate — more formal; means to grow rapidly in intensity
  • get out of control — essentially the same meaning, less idiomatic
Words and Phrases That Mean the Opposite (Antonyms)

• be under control — "Don't worry, the situation is under control."
  • be in hand — the original opposite phrase; still used in British English
  • be manageable — "The workload is still manageable."
  • be kept in check — "The crowds were kept in check by security."
Formal or Informal? Where Can You Use It?

This idiom sits comfortably in both informal and semi-formal contexts. You can use it:

  • In casual conversation with friends
  • In workplace conversations or emails
  • In news reporting and journalism
  • In speeches or presentations

You would generally avoid it in very strict academic or legal writing, where plain, precise language is preferred (like "the situation became unmanageable"). But in almost every other setting, it is perfectly appropriate.
A Simple Way to Never Forget This Idiom

Picture a person trying to hold too many balloons. At first, they're managing fine. Then the wind picks up. One balloon escapes. Then another. Then all of them fly away in every direction. That moment when they all fly away and there's nothing left to hold? That's exactly when things have gotten out of hand.

Control was there. And then it wasn't.

That is everything you need to know about the idiom "get out of hand" — its meaning, origin, grammar, usage, examples, and nuances — all in one place.
6884:
To get one's back up means to become angry, irritated, or defensive about something. When someone's back is up, they feel annoyed and are ready to push back or argue. Think of it as the moment a person shifts from being calm to being on edge — bristling, touchy, and not willing to back down.

The phrase works in two directions:

1. You can get your own back up — meaning you become irritated or defensive.

"Don't get your back up — I was only asking a simple question."

2. You can get someone else's back up — meaning your actions or words cause another person to become irritated or defensive.

"His dismissive attitude really got my back up."
"Try not to get the boss's back up before the meeting."
Where Does It Come From? (The Origin)

This phrase is born from one of the most familiar sights in nature — an angry cat.

When a cat feels threatened, startled, or furious, it arches its back upward, puffs up its fur, and stands rigid. This posture is an unmistakable signal: "I am angry. Back off." You have almost certainly seen a cat do this.

Centuries ago, people noticed this exact behavior and began using it as a metaphor for human anger and defensiveness. Just as the cat raises its back when provoked, a person who is irritated or defensive is said to have their "back up." The image is vivid and makes the phrase very easy to remember — picture that arched, bristling cat, and you will never forget what this expression means.

The phrase has been in use in the English language since at least the early 1700s, making it a well-established, time-tested idiom.
The Nuance: Anger and Defensiveness Together

What makes this phrase particularly interesting is that it captures two feelings at once — anger and defensiveness — which often go hand in hand.

When someone's back is up, they are not just quietly annoyed. They are reacting. They feel that they have been attacked, criticized, disrespected, or provoked, and they are now on guard — ready to defend themselves or fight back. It is the emotional equivalent of the cat's arched back: a signal that says "You have crossed a line, and I am not happy about it."

This is slightly different from pure anger. For example:

  • If you spill coffee and get frustrated, that is just ordinary anger.
  • But if someone insults your work and you feel both hurt and ready to argue back, that is when your back is up.

The phrase almost always carries this sense of being triggered by someone or something external — it is a reaction to a provocation, not just a random mood.
All the Common Forms You Will Encounter

The phrase appears in several related forms. Here they all are, so nothing catches you off guard:

"Get one's back up" — to become annoyed/defensive (most common form)

"I got my back up when he questioned my honesty."

"Put one's back up" — exact same meaning, very common especially in British English

"His tone immediately put my back up."

"Get someone's back up" — to cause another person to become annoyed or defensive

"Bringing up the old argument will only get her back up."

"Put someone's back up" — again, same meaning as above

"The new policy has put everyone's back up."

"Have one's back up" — to already be in a state of irritation (describing a current state rather than the moment it happens)

"He's had his back up all morning — something must have gone wrong."

All of these forms are correct and natural. The differences are tiny (just the verb choice and whose back is being raised), and the core meaning stays the same across all of them.

Seeing a phrase in realistic situations is the fastest way to truly absorb it. Here are several:

"I didn't mean to criticize your cooking — please don't get your back up about it."

(Don't take offense; stay calm.)

"The journalist's aggressive questioning really got the politician's back up."

(The aggressive questions irritated and put the politician on the defensive.)

"She had her back up from the moment she walked into the room — clearly, something had already upset her."

(She was already in an irritated, defensive state.)

"I know he's wrong, but pointing it out in public will only put his back up and make things worse."

(Correcting him publicly will just make him angry and defensive, not cooperative.)

"I try not to let small things get my back up, but that kind of rudeness is hard to ignore."

(I try not to get easily annoyed, but that rudeness was difficult to overlook.)
The Register: When and Where to Use It

This phrase is informal and colloquial, meaning it belongs in everyday conversation and casual writing. It is perfectly natural when:

  • Talking with friends, family, or colleagues.
  • Writing an informal email or text message.
  • Writing fiction or dialogue.

It would feel out of place in very formal writing, such as an academic paper, a legal document, or an official report. In those contexts, you would simply write "irritated," "offended," or "defensive" instead.

The phrase is widely used in British, Australian, Canadian, and American English, so it is understood across the English-speaking world.
How It Differs from Similar Phrases

It helps to know how this phrase sits alongside related expressions:

  • "Rub someone the wrong way" — to mildly or gradually annoy someone, often without meaning to. Less intense than getting someone's back up; no defensive posture implied.
  • "Get under someone's skin" — to irritate someone persistently, often in a way that is hard to shake off.
  • "Get someone's hackles up" — nearly identical in meaning to "get one's back up." Hackles are the hairs on the back of a dog's or cat's neck that stand up when the animal is angry — so same animal imagery, same idea. The two phrases are virtually interchangeable.
  • "Get a rise out of someone" — to deliberately provoke someone into an angry reaction, often for amusement.

Of these, "get someone's hackles up" is the closest relative — almost a twin of the phrase you are learning.

If you ever need to recall this phrase in a flash, remember this:

"Get one's back up" = to become (or to make someone) angry and defensive, just like a cat arching its back when threatened.

That image of the arched cat is your anchor. Every time you hear this phrase, picture that cat — and the meaning will come to you instantly.
6885:
To get the better of someone means to defeat, overcome, or gain an advantage over someone or something.

Think of it as a contest. Two sides are competing — and one side wins. The winner has "got the better of" the loser.

But here is the interesting part: the "someone" in this idiom doesn't always have to be another person. It can also be your own emotion or feeling that defeats you. This is what makes this idiom so rich and widely used.

The key word here is "better." In everyday English, we often use "better" to mean "improved" (e.g., I feel better today). But in this idiom, "better" is used in an older sense, meaning "advantage" or "superiority."

So, "get the better of someone" literally means "gain the advantage over someone."

The phrase "the better" refers to the winning position — the upper hand in a contest.

This idiom works in two distinct situations. Understanding both will give you complete mastery of it.

Use 1: One Person Defeats or Outsmarks Another

This is the most straightforward use. It describes a situation — a competition, an argument, a fight, a game — where one person clearly wins over another.

Examples:

  • "Despite being younger and less experienced, she got the better of her opponent in the debate."
    → She won the debate. Her opponent couldn't match her.
  • "The detective got the better of the criminal by setting a clever trap."
    → The detective outsmarted the criminal and won.
  • "No one in the class could get the better of him at chess."
    → Nobody could beat him at chess.

Notice that in all these cases, there is a clear winner and a clear loser. The winner has "got the better of" the loser.

Use 2: An Emotion or Feeling Defeats a Person

This is the more powerful and poetic use of the idiom. Here, the "someone" being defeated is you — and the thing that defeats you is not another person, but your own emotion, instinct, or feeling.

In this use, the idiom means: "A feeling became so strong that you could not control it. It took over."

Examples:

  • "Curiosity got the better of him, and he opened the letter he was told not to read."
    → He couldn't resist. His curiosity was stronger than his willpower.
  • "Fear got the better of her before the interview, and she forgot everything she had prepared."
    → Fear overpowered her. She lost control.
  • "His anger got the better of him, and he said things he later regretted."
    → His anger took over. His rational mind lost.
  • "Don't let jealousy get the better of you."
    → Don't allow jealousy to control you or make you do something you shouldn't.

The important nuance here: In this use, there is almost always a slightly negative tone. The person should have stayed in control, but they didn't. The emotion won when it shouldn't have. This is why phrases like "don't let [emotion] get the better of you" are so common — they are warnings to stay in control.
Grammar: How to Use It Correctly

Basic structure:

[Subject] + got/get/gets + the better of + [object]

The subject can be:

  • A person (She got the better of him)
  • An emotion (Fear got the better of her)

The object can be:

  • A person (...of him / of her / of the champion)
  • A reflexive pronoun (...of me / of yourself)

Tense variations:

Example
PastHis nerves got the better of him.
PresentShe always gets the better of her rivals.
InfinitiveDon't let greed get the better of you.

The past tense ("got the better of") is by far the most common form you will encounter and use.

These phrases share the same core idea:

  • Get the upper hand — to gain an advantage over someone
  • Gain the advantage over — to move into a superior position
  • Overcome — to successfully deal with or defeat something
  • Best someone — (formal) to defeat someone
  • Outdo someone — to do better than someone
  • Prevail over — to win or prove superior

Among these, "get the upper hand" is the closest equivalent to Use 1 (defeating another person), while "overcome" is closest to Use 2 (when an emotion controls you).
What This Idiom Does NOT Mean

It's important to clarify a few things learners sometimes confuse:

1. It does NOT mean simply "to be better than someone" in a general, ongoing sense.
Saying "She is better at cooking than him" is different from "She got the better of him in the cook-off." The idiom always implies a specific contest or moment of victory, not just a general comparison.

2. It does NOT require a physical fight.
You can get the better of someone in a conversation, a card game, a legal case, a negotiation, or even a staring contest. The "contest" can be anything.

3. "Got the better of" does NOT mean the loser is permanently defeated.
It just means they lost in that particular moment or situation. Next time, the result might be different.
Remembering It with a Mental Image

Imagine two people in a tug-of-war. The rope is the contest — it could be an argument, a game, or even your own self-control. Whoever pulls the other person over the line has "got the better of" them.

Now imagine that one of the "people" on the other end of the rope is your own anger or fear. If you get pulled over the line, your emotion has got the better of you.

"Get the better of someone" = to defeat, overcome, or gain control over someone or something.

It has two main uses:

  1. One person defeats or outsmarks another person in a contest.
  2. An emotion or feeling takes control of a person against their better judgment.

The phrase carries the idea of a competition with a clear winner. Whether that winner is another person or your own uncontrolled emotion, they have successfully "got the better of" whoever or whatever was on the other side.
6886:
When someone "gets the wrong end of the stick," it means they have completely misunderstood a situation, a message, or what someone said. They heard or saw something, but walked away with the wrong idea about it.

It is not about lying. It is not about ignoring something. It is specifically about misunderstanding — genuinely believing something that is incorrect because you interpreted things the wrong way.

Think of it like this: someone gives you a puzzle, but you solve the wrong puzzle entirely. You were confident, you put in effort, but you started from a wrong assumption.
A Simple Example to Make It Crystal Clear

Imagine your friend says:

"I heard that Tom was talking about you at the party."

You assume Tom was saying bad things about you. You get upset. You avoid Tom for a week.

Later, you find out Tom was actually praising you — telling everyone how talented you are.

You got the wrong end of the stick. You misread the situation completely. The information was innocent, but you interpreted it in the worst possible way.
Where Did This Idiom Come From?

This is where it gets interesting. There are a couple of theories, and knowing them will help the meaning stick in your memory forever.

Theory 1 — The Walking Stick (Most Common Explanation)

In the old days, people commonly used long walking sticks or staffs. If two people were handling a stick together, one person naturally held the top end (the clean, proper end — the "right" end), while the other, by mistake or confusion, grabbed the bottom end (the dirty, muddy end that drags on the ground — the "wrong" end).

The person with the wrong end was at a disadvantage and had misread which end to hold. This became a metaphor for misreading a situation.

Theory 2 — The Unpleasant Historical Origin (More Vivid)

Some language historians point to a more graphic and memorable origin. Before modern plumbing existed, people used a stick with a cloth or sponge at one end to clean themselves after using the toilet (much like ancient Romans did with a sponge-on-a-stick called a xylospongium).

If you picked up that stick from the wrong end — the dirty end — by mistake, the result was extremely unpleasant and completely your own fault for not paying attention.

Grabbing that wrong end = a big, embarrassing mistake caused entirely by misunderstanding. The metaphor transferred perfectly into everyday language.

Both origins point to the same core idea: you picked up something from the wrong side because you misjudged it.
The Full Form of the Idiom

You will sometimes hear people say the slightly longer version:

"get hold of the wrong end of the stick"

This is the same idiom. The word hold is sometimes added for emphasis, but the meaning is identical. Both versions are correct and widely used.
Important Things to Know About This Idiom

1. It is British English.
This phrase is used far more commonly in British English than in American English. Americans are more likely to say "get the wrong idea" or "misread the situation." However, people all around the world who speak English will understand it.

2. It is informal.
You would use it in conversation, in casual writing, in a text message, or in a story — but not in a formal report or a legal document.

3. It is not insulting by nature.
Saying someone "got the wrong end of the stick" is usually sympathetic or gently humorous, not cruel. It acknowledges that the misunderstanding was understandable, even if it led to a funny or awkward situation. However, depending on your tone, it can be used critically too.

4. The misunderstanding is genuine.
The person who "gets the wrong end of the stick" is not lying and not pretending. They truly believed their wrong interpretation. That is what separates this from deception.

Here are several examples across different situations so you can see how naturally this idiom fits into everyday language:

  • "She got the wrong end of the stick and thought the party was a surprise for her, but it was actually for her sister."
  • "He got the wrong end of the stick when he read my email. I said the project needs more time — he thought I meant I wanted to cancel it entirely."
  • "Don't get the wrong end of the stick — I'm not criticising your work. I'm just suggesting a small change."
  • "The media completely got the wrong end of the stick with the politician's speech and reported something he never actually said."
  • "I got the wrong end of the stick and prepared a presentation for the wrong meeting. I was so embarrassed."

Notice how in every example, the key ingredients are the same: a misunderstanding, a wrong conclusion drawn from something real, and genuine belief in that wrong conclusion.
How Is It Different From Similar Phrases?

It helps to know how this idiom compares to expressions that seem similar but aren't quite the same:

  • "Bark up the wrong tree" — means you are pursuing the wrong person or solution, not just misunderstanding something. It's about going in the wrong direction with your actions.
  • "Miss the point" — means you failed to understand the most important part of something. It's close, but "get the wrong end of the stick" usually implies you've replaced the correct understanding with a completely wrong one, not just that you missed the key point.
  • "Jump to conclusions" — means you decided something too quickly, without enough information. "Get the wrong end of the stick" can happen slowly too, not just hastily.
  • "Get the wrong idea" — this is the closest American English equivalent. They mean almost the same thing, but "get the wrong idea" is more universal, while "get the wrong end of the stick" is more colourful and distinctly British.
A Quick Way to Remember It Forever

Picture this scene in your mind:

You reach out to grab a stick. One end is clean and smooth. The other end is dirty and unpleasant. You grab the dirty end by mistake — and now you're stuck holding something in completely the wrong way, through no one's fault but your own misreading of the situation.

That image = misunderstanding something completely.

Every time you hear the phrase, let that image flash in your mind, and the meaning will come back to you instantly.
"Get the wrong end of the stick" means to completely misunderstand a situation, a message, or what someone meant — arriving at a wrong conclusion that feels real to you, but is simply incorrect.
6887:
To "get to grips with" something means to make a serious effort to understand, deal with, or take control of something that is difficult, unfamiliar, or challenging.

When you "get to grips with" something, you stop avoiding it or feeling confused by it, and instead you engage with it directly and tackle it properly.

Think of it this way: if something is hard to understand or handle, and you finally sit down, put in effort, and start making sense of it — that is exactly what this idiom describes.

The word "grip" literally means to hold something tightly and firmly with your hand. Picture someone grabbing a rope, a tool, or an opponent in a wrestling match — they have a firm, controlled hold on it.

The idiom is rooted in this physical image. Just like a wrestler needs to get a firm grip on their opponent to gain control, we use the same idea for mental and practical challenges. When you "get to grips with" a difficult problem, you are metaphorically grabbing hold of it firmly instead of letting it slip away from you.

This is why the idiom carries a sense of active effort and control — it's not passive. You are the one reaching out, grabbing the problem, and wrestling with it.
The Full Breakdown of What It Implies

When someone says they need to "get to grips with" something, it usually implies three things at once:

1. There is difficulty involved.
The thing in question is not easy. It is complex, new, overwhelming, or unfamiliar. You wouldn't say you need to "get to grips with" tying your shoelaces — that's too simple.

2. An effort must be made.
The phrase suggests that you need to invest real time, focus, and energy. It's not something that happens automatically.

3. The goal is understanding or control.
The end result of "getting to grips with" something is that you understand it properly, or you are able to handle it effectively. You go from being lost or overwhelmed to being in command.

Here are examples across different situations so you can see how naturally this idiom fits into real life:

Learning something new:
"I have just started learning Python. It's taking me a while to get to grips with all the syntax."

A new job or responsibility:
"She has just been promoted to manager. She needs to get to grips with the new role quickly."

A difficult subject:
"Many students find it hard to get to grips with quantum physics."

A complex situation:
"The government is struggling to get to grips with the housing crisis."

A new piece of technology:
"My grandfather finally got to grips with his new smartphone after a few weeks of practice."

An emotional challenge:
"After losing his job, it took him some time to get to grips with his new reality."

Notice how in every single example, there is something difficult, new, or overwhelming, and the person is working to understand or handle it properly.
"Get to Grips With" vs. "Come to Grips With"

You will often hear both versions, and they are very close in meaning. Here is the subtle difference:

"Get to grips with" is more commonly used when talking about understanding or practically dealing with something — a skill, a task, a concept, a system.

"I need to get to grips with this new accounting software."

"Come to grips with" is more commonly used when talking about emotionally accepting a difficult truth or reality — a loss, a hard fact, a painful situation.

"She is still coming to grips with the death of her father."

That said, in everyday conversation, many native speakers use them interchangeably, and you will rarely be misunderstood either way.

Here are other idioms and phrases with a similar meaning, so you can recognise them when you encounter them:

"Get a handle on" — to begin to understand or control something.
"I'm trying to get a handle on my finances."

"Wrap your head around" — to fully understand something difficult or strange.
"I can't wrap my head around this theory."

"Come to terms with" — to accept something difficult emotionally.
"He came to terms with his illness."

"Grapple with" — to struggle to deal with or understand something.
"She is grappling with a tough decision."

All of these share the spirit of struggling with something hard and working through it, just like "get to grips with."
Register: When and Where Is It Used?

This idiom is completely natural in both formal and informal settings. You can use it in:

  • Everyday conversation with friends and colleagues
  • Professional emails and reports
  • News articles and academic writing
  • Speeches and presentations

It is most common in British English, but it is well understood and used in all varieties of English worldwide.

It is important to understand a few things this idiom does not mean:

  • It does not mean you have already mastered something. "Getting to grips with" is the process, not the finished achievement.
  • It does not carry a negative judgement. Saying someone needs to "get to grips with" something is not an insult — it simply means there is a challenge they need to work through.
  • It does not mean a quick or instant thing. It usually implies a period of effort and adjustment.

Core meaningTo seriously try to understand, deal with, or take control of something difficult
ToneNeutral; works in formal and informal contexts
OriginFrom the physical idea of gripping something firmly to gain control
Common contextsLearning, work, emotions, complex situations
Close relative"Come to grips with" (more emotional); "get a handle on" (very similar)
One Final Way to Remember It

Imagine someone handed you a large, slippery, awkward box. At first, you fumble with it — your hands keep slipping, you can't hold it properly. Then, after some effort, you get a firm grip on it and carry it with confidence.

That fumbling-then-gripping moment is exactly what "getting to grips with" something feels like — you go from confusion and struggle to confidence and control.
6888:
This idiom has two meanings — and they are surprisingly different from each other. This is one of the most interesting things about it. The meaning changes completely depending on the context.

Meaning 1 — To irritate or bother someone deeply
When something or someone "gets under your skin," it means they annoy or disturb you in a deep, persistent way. Not just a small, passing irritation — but the kind that sticks with you and is hard to shake off.

Meaning 2 — To deeply affect or captivate someone (usually in a romantic or emotional way)
When a person "gets under your skin" in this sense, it means they have touched your heart or emotions so deeply that you can't stop thinking about them. You are drawn to them powerfully, almost without being able to control it.
Where Does the Phrase Come From?

The image behind this idiom is physical and very vivid. Think about what happens when a splinter, a thorn, or an insect gets literally under your skin. It is stuck. You can't ignore it. It keeps bothering you from the inside, no matter what you do. You can't easily pull it out.

This physical feeling — of something being trapped inside you, nagging at you — is exactly what the idiom captures. Whether it is annoyance that won't go away, or a person you can't stop thinking about, the idea is the same: something has gotten inside you, beyond the surface, and it won't let go.
Breaking Down Both Meanings in Detail

Meaning 1 — Irritation and Annoyance

When something "gets under your skin" in the negative sense, it means it bothers you more than it probably should. It bypasses your patience and affects you on a deeper level.

This can be caused by:

  • A person's habit or behavior
  • A repetitive sound or situation
  • A comment someone made
  • An ongoing problem

Examples:

  • "My coworker chews his food so loudly. It really gets under my skin."
  • "She knows exactly what to say to get under my skin."
  • "Don't let their rude comments get under your skin. They're not worth it."
  • "The constant noise from the street is starting to get under my skin."

Notice how in all of these, the irritation is deep and hard to ignore — not just a tiny, forgettable bother.

Meaning 2 — Deep Emotional Captivation

This is the warmer, more romantic meaning. When a person "gets under your skin" this way, they have entered your thoughts and emotions in a way you didn't expect or can't easily control. You find yourself thinking about them constantly. They have affected you profoundly.

This meaning was made globally famous by Cole Porter's 1936 classic song "I've Got You Under My Skin," where the singer describes being so deeply, helplessly drawn to someone that they have become a part of him.

Examples:

  • "I don't know what it is about her, but she's really gotten under my skin."
  • "That film got under my skin. I'm still thinking about it three days later."
  • "He wasn't even my type, but somehow he got under my skin."
  • "This book has really gotten under my skin — I can't put it down."

Note that this meaning isn't always about romance. It can also apply to a piece of music, a book, a film, or even an idea — anything that affects you deeply and stays with you.
How Do You Know Which Meaning Is Being Used?

Context is everything. Here are two simple rules of thumb:

  • If the sentence carries a negative, frustrated, or tired tone, it almost certainly means irritation.
  • If the sentence carries a warm, wistful, or amazed tone, it almost certainly means deep emotional captivation.

Compare these two sentences:

  • "His arrogance really gets under my skin." → Annoyance
  • "Her kindness has gotten under my skin." → Deep emotional impact

The structure is flexible. Here are the patterns you'll commonly see:

  • gets under my / your / his / her / our / their skin (present tense)
  • got under my skin (past tense)
  • has gotten / has got under my skin (present perfect)
  • is getting under my skin (present continuous — for something happening now)

You will almost always see a possessive pronoun in the middle (my, your, his, her, etc.) to show whose skin is being referred to.
Register — When and Where Is This Used?

This is an informal, everyday expression. You will hear it in:

  • Casual conversations
  • Informal writing (blogs, texts, social media)
  • Novels, films, and song lyrics

You would not use it in formal academic writing or professional reports. Stick to it in everyday speech and informal contexts.
Similar Expressions (To Round Out Your Understanding)

For the irritation meaning, similar expressions include:

  • "Get on someone's nerves" — She gets on my nerves.
  • "Rub someone the wrong way" — His attitude rubs me the wrong way.
  • "Drive someone up the wall" — That sound drives me up the wall.

For the captivation meaning, similar expressions include:

  • "Grow on someone" — Her music has really grown on me.
  • "Can't get someone out of your head" — I can't get him out of my head.

Meaning 1To deeply irritate or bother someone
Meaning 2To deeply captivate or emotionally affect someone
Key imageA splinter stuck beneath your skin — something inside you that won't go away
Tone clueNegative context = irritation / Warm context = captivation
RegisterInformal

The beauty of this idiom is that the same words can describe two very different kinds of feeling — because in both cases, something has moved past your surface and settled inside you. Whether that feels like a thorn or a heartbeat depends entirely on the situation.
6889:
To get wind of something means to hear about or find out about something — especially a piece of information that was secret, private, or not meant for you.

The key idea is that you discovered the information indirectly — not because someone told you directly, but because you happened to hear it, sense it, or pick it up through some informal channel (gossip, rumour, overhearing, etc.).

Think of it this way: you didn't walk through the front door — you caught a scent drifting through the air. That is the spirit of this idiom.

This idiom comes from the world of animals and hunting.

Animals like deer, wolves, and rabbits have a powerful sense of smell. When the wind blows in their direction, they can smell a predator or a hunter from far away — before they can even see or hear them. By "getting wind" of the danger, they become aware of it and can react.

Over time, people borrowed this idea and applied it to information. Just like an animal catches a scent carried by the wind, a person can "catch" a piece of news or information that is drifting around — without it being handed to them directly.

get wind of + something

The "something" is always a piece of information, a plan, a secret, or news — something that is typically private or sensitive.

1. A workplace scenario:

"The employees started working extra hard because they got wind of a surprise inspection by the manager."

Here, nobody officially told the employees about the inspection. They found out through whispers or gossip. That informal discovery is exactly what "got wind of" captures.

2. A business scenario:

"The rival company got wind of our new product launch and rushed to release something similar first."

The rival wasn't supposed to know. They found out somehow — perhaps through a leaked email, a former employee, or industry gossip.

3. A personal/family scenario:

"I was planning a surprise birthday party for my mom, but she got wind of it and pretended to be surprised anyway."

The mom discovered the secret before she was supposed to. She didn't find out because someone sat her down and told her — she picked it up casually and indirectly.

4. A news/journalism scenario:

"The journalist got wind of the corruption scandal months before it became public."

The journalist heard about it through sources, tips, or unofficial channels — not through an official press release.
The Tone and Feeling of This Idiom

This idiom almost always carries one or more of these feelings:

  • Secrecy — the information was private or hidden.
  • Surprise — someone found out who wasn't supposed to, or found out earlier than expected.
  • Informality — the discovery happened through casual, unofficial means.
  • A hint of drama — because secrets being discovered often changes things.

It is rarely used for information that is public or openly shared. You would not say "I got wind of the fact that the sun rises in the east." That is common knowledge. The idiom works best when there is an element of discovery of something hidden.

It does not mean:

  • Being officially informed of something (use "was told" or "was notified" for that).
  • Learning something from a textbook or formal source.
  • Smelling something with your nose (even though the origin is about smell, the idiom today is entirely about information, not actual wind or odours).

The idiom is flexible across tenses:

  • Past: "She got wind of the plan." (most common)
  • Present: "He's getting wind of our secret."
  • Future/Conditional: "If they get wind of this, we're in trouble."
  • Negative: "We have to make sure no one gets wind of this." (very common — often used to warn against a secret leaking)

The negative form ("make sure no one gets wind of it") is extremely common in everyday English, often used when someone is trying to keep something secret.
Similar Idioms (So You Can Tell Them Apart)

IdiomMeaningDifference

"Catch wind of" — This is simply another way of saying the exact same thing. "I caught wind of the rumour" = "I got wind of the rumour." They are interchangeable.

"Hear on the grapevine" — Also means learning something informally through gossip. Very similar in meaning to "get wind of," but "grapevine" specifically emphasizes the chain of gossip (person to person), while "get wind of" is slightly broader — it can include overhearing, sensing, or any indirect means.

"Catch a whiff of" — Again comes from smell. In informal English, it can mean the same as "get wind of" but it's used less commonly.

Picture a fox sniffing the air. It can't see the chicken coop, it can't hear anything — but the wind carries a scent, and now the fox knows something is nearby.

You = the fox.
The secret information = the scent on the wind.

When you get wind of something, you are that fox — you picked up on something that was floating quietly through the air, not meant for you to know.
"Get wind of something" means to discover or hear about something — especially a secret or private piece of information — through informal, indirect, or unintended means.
